summary: Describes how to configure Microsoft Word to produce Internet Drafts and RFCs. It was replaced by RFC 5385.

eli5.summary: Steps for making Word write documents in the special style used for RFCs. It has been replaced by RFC 5385.

subtitle: How to set up Microsoft Word to produce RFC-compliant documents

tldr.problem: Creating Internet Drafts and RFCs requires exact formatting: 72 characters per line, 58 lines per page, specific line endings (CRLF), and careful handling of headers, footers and section numbering.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3285 provides step-by-step instructions to configure Microsoft Word with custom styles and page layout, then use the CRLF program to fix line termination in the final output.
tldr.outcome: Authors could use Word's WYSIWYG editor to draft RFCs while producing correctly formatted text files suitable for submission. It was replaced by RFC 5385.

today: RFC 3285 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 5385, which provides updated guidance on producing RFCs and Internet Drafts. However, the technique described—configuring Word to produce RFC-compliant output—was used by RFC authors during the period when these tools were current.

sections.title: Creating RFCs with Microsoft Word
sections.content:
RFC 3285 describes how to configure Microsoft Word 97 and later to produce Internet Drafts and RFCs that comply with IETF submission specifications. The RFC is unsupported and was developed by the authors while employed at Microsoft, but is not a Microsoft product.

The challenge is that RFCs require exact formatting: 72 characters per line, 58 lines per page, each line terminated with carriage return and line feed (CRLF), and specific handling of page breaks. Using Word's default settings produces documents with incorrect line breaks and formatting. This RFC provides a complete guide to customize Word so it can be used as a WYSIWYG editor while producing correctly formatted text files.
sections.eli5: Word normally makes documents that don't match RFC rules. This RFC says how to change Word's settings so your document comes out RFC-formatted when you save it.

sections.title: Configuring Word Page Layout and Styles
sections.content:
The core solution involves defining two custom styles in Word: RFC Heading and RFC Text. These styles must use Courier New font at 12 points with exact line spacing of 12 points.

Page layout settings control the line width and page height. The right margin is set to 93.6 points to achieve 72 characters per line using 12-point font at 10 characters per inch. The paper height is set to 660 points (12 points × 55 lines) to achieve 55 lines per page, which accounts for spacing at the top of the page. Top margin is 24 points, while bottom, left, and right margins are set to 0, 0, and 93.6 points respectively.

Tab stops must be set at every 3 spaces to support indentation and alignment within text. Headers and footers are configured to be different on the first page, with specific tabs for centering and right-alignment at 252 and 504 points.
sections.eli5: You set up two special styles—one for headings, one for body text. Then you tell Word exactly how wide to make lines and how tall to make pages using very specific measurements.

sections.title: Automatic Numbering and Headers
sections.content:
RFC 3285 describes how to use Word's built-in features for automatic reference numbering, table of contents generation, and date fields to keep drafts current.

For automatic dates, an insert field with SAVEDATE \@ "MMMM YYYY" format places the current save date, which displays with a gray background in editing mode but prints normally. For expiration dates six months ahead, the RFC shows how to nest IF fields that test the current month and return the appropriate expiration month. These fields update automatically when the document is saved.

For reference numbering, the document is divided into sections, and endnotes are configured to auto-number as [1], [2], etc. Cross-references can be inserted to link to earlier footnotes, and all numbers update automatically as the document changes.
sections.eli5: Word can automatically put today's date on your document. For the expiration date, you write a formula that figures out what date is six months away. Reference numbers update by themselves too.

sections.title: The CRLF Program and Line Termination
sections.content:
When Word prints to the Generic Text Printer driver and saves to a file, some blank lines are terminated with only a line feed (LF) instead of carriage return plus line feed (CRLF), because printers do not need to move the print head for blank lines.

RFC 3285 includes C source code for a CRLF.EXE program that fixes this. The program reads the text file produced by printing and processes each byte. It handles four main cases: form feeds that appear without proper CRLF framing, carriage returns that need line feeds appended, line feeds that appear without preceding carriage returns, and blank lines within pages. The program ensures that every line ends with CRLF and every page ends with CRLF followed by a form feed.

The usage is simple: crlf source.prn destination.txt. The RFC also notes that the code is provided as a basis for customization, since different versions of Windows have slightly different Generic Printer drivers.
sections.eli5: When you print Word to a file, it sometimes messes up the line breaks. A helper program reads the file and fixes all the line breaks to match RFC rules.

sections.title: Known Issues and Workarounds
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main problems that have been reported by users.

Margin clipping occurred in some version combinations of Windows and Word, where characters on the left side of the line were cut off during printing. Shifting both left and right margins to the right by equal amounts (for example, 36 and 57.6 points instead of 0 and 93.6) resolves the clipping, though it adds leading spaces to the file.

Printing the draft to an actual printer (rather than to a file using the Generic Text printer) produces an error message about margins being outside the printable area, and the first two characters of headings are truncated. The RFC recommends producing printed copies by creating a text file with the CRLF program and redirecting it to the printer, or reopening the text file in Word with all margins set to 0.65 inches.

The underscore character appears as a blank space on most screens when used in RFC Text and RFC Heading styles, but prints correctly in the final output.
sections.eli5: Sometimes Word clips characters off the left, sometimes printing doesn't work right, and sometimes underscores look weird on screen even though they print fine.
